title: Empire & the Literary
description: How colonialism shaped the canon — what postcolonial criticism does

concepts.title: What Postcolonial Criticism Does
concepts.contentHtml:
Postcolonial criticism examines colonialism's effects on culture — both during empire and afterward. The 'post' is uncertain: many former colonies remain economically subordinate, and colonial categories shape thought decades after formal independence.

The field developed from the 1970s through writers including Edward Said, Gayatri Spivak, Homi Bhabha, and the long preceding tradition of Frantz Fanon, C.L.R. James, Aimé Césaire.

Major moves: rereading the European canon for its colonial assumptions; recovering and centring writing from former colonies; analysing the cultural mechanisms of colonisation and decolonisation.

concepts.title: Empire in the Canon
concepts.contentHtml:
Edward Said's Culture and Imperialism (1993) showed how Austen's Mansfield Park, set in part on the income from a Caribbean plantation, registers and obscures the slavery that funds the household.

Conrad's Heart of Darkness, Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, Kipling's verse, Forster's A Passage to India — all repay rereading with attention to the colonial frame.

The point isn't to dismiss canonical works but to read them more carefully. Empire is in the canon whether the canon acknowledges it or not.

concepts.title: Frantz Fanon
concepts.contentHtml:
Frantz Fanon (1925-1961) was the great theorist of decolonisation. Born in Martinique, trained as a psychiatrist in France, he worked in Algeria during the war of independence and supported the FLN.

His major books: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) on the psychological effects of colonisation; The Wretched of the Earth (1961) on the violent dynamics of decolonisation.

Fanon argued that colonisation is not just political and economic but psychological — colonised people internalise the coloniser's view of themselves. He was suspicious of national-bourgeoisie post-independence elites who would simply replace European masters.

concepts.title: Other Foundations
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond Fanon:

Aimé Césaire (Martinique, 1913-2008): poet, statesman, theorist of Négritude. Discourse on Colonialism (1950) excoriated European colonialism.

C.L.R. James (Trinidad, 1901-1989): historian, novelist, critic. The Black Jacobins (1938) on the Haitian Revolution.

Albert Memmi (Tunisia, 1920-2020): The Colonizer and the Colonized (1957).

The Caribbean and North African writers established the foundations on which Said and the Anglo-American academic field would later build.

concepts.title: What's at Stake
concepts.contentHtml:
Postcolonial criticism has been criticised — sometimes from the right, sometimes from within the broader left.

Right critique: that the field is anti-Western, treats European canon dismissively, projects 21st-century politics back onto 19th-century texts.

Left critique: that postcolonial theory has become academically institutionalised in ways that blunt its political force.

Defenders: empire genuinely shapes culture; the literary canon is unintelligible without that frame; recovering writing from former colonies has expanded what literature looks like in productive ways.

title: Said & Orientalism
description: Representations of the East as ideological project

concepts.title: Said
concepts.contentHtml:
Edward Said (1935-2003), Palestinian-American literary critic at Columbia, was the founding figure of academic postcolonial studies.

Major works: Orientalism (1978), The World, the Text, and the Critic (1983), Culture and Imperialism (1993). Plus extensive political writing on Palestine.

Said's combination of literary scholarship with political engagement was unusual in his American academic context.

concepts.title: Orientalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Orientalism (1978) is the founding text of the field.

Said's argument: European scholarly representations of 'the Orient' formed a coherent system of knowledge — what Foucault would call a discourse — that served imperial domination. The system created the East as fundamentally different from, and inferior to, the West. Sensual, despotic, irrational, feminine, in need of rule.

This wasn't conscious propaganda. It was a structure of assumption built into philology, history, area studies, novels, travel writing, paintings.

concepts.title: Reception and Criticism
concepts.contentHtml:
The book's reception was massive and divided.

Defenders: Said had identified a real pattern. The connection between knowledge and power Said traced is genuinely there.

Critics: Said overgeneralised. Specific Orientalists (Lane) had genuine respect for cultures studied. The 'Orient' is too varied (China, Japan, India, the Arab world) to be treated as one object.

Most contemporary scholarship treats Said as productive but partial. The framework remains essential; the specific historical claims need refinement case by case.

concepts.title: Culture and Imperialism
concepts.contentHtml:
Said's later Culture and Imperialism (1993) extended the analysis to the relationship between European literature and empire.

The central method: contrapuntal reading. Reading Western canonical works alongside the colonised perspectives they presuppose but rarely articulate.

The book broadened the scope from the Orient to imperial culture more generally. It also engaged music (Verdi's Aida) and contemporary politics.

concepts.title: Said's Influence
concepts.contentHtml:
Said's combination of literary close reading with political-historical analysis became a model for the field.

The terms 'Orientalism' and 'contrapuntal reading' have entered general academic vocabulary. The method has become standard.

His political writing on Palestine made him a public intellectual on a scale unusual for literary academics. He died of leukemia in 2003. His memoir Out of Place (1999) is one of the great literary autobiographies of recent decades.

title: Achebe & African Voices
description: Things Fall Apart and writing back to empire

concepts.title: Things Fall Apart
concepts.contentHtml:
Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) is the founding text of modern African Anglophone literature. The novel depicts Igbo society in late-19th-century Nigeria through the rise and fall of Okonkwo, a respected warrior and farmer.

The novel's first two-thirds present Igbo life on its own terms — its religion, customs, family structures, social hierarchies. The arrival of British colonisers and Christian missionaries disrupts everything. Okonkwo's resistance leads to his death.

The achievement: depicting a colonised society as it understood itself, before and through the encounter with empire.

concepts.title: Achebe and Conrad
concepts.contentHtml:
Achebe's 1975 lecture 'An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness' provoked enduring debate. He argued that Heart of Darkness uses Africa as a setting for European existential crisis, treating Africans as undifferentiated savages without speech, history, or interiority.

The argument has been disputed. Defenders of Conrad note the novel's anti-imperial themes, its critical stance toward European brutality.

The debate has been productive. It changed how Heart of Darkness is taught.

concepts.title: Other African Anglophones
concepts.contentHtml:
Achebe opened a tradition.

Wole Soyinka (Nigerian, b. 1934, Nobel 1986): playwright, poet, essayist.

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o (Kenyan, b. 1938): switched from English to Gikuyu in the late 1970s. Decolonising the Mind (1986) is the classic argument for African-language literature.

Bessie Head (South African / Botswanan, 1937-1986).

Nadine Gordimer (South African, Nobel 1991).

J.M. Coetzee (South African, Nobel 2003): Disgrace, Waiting for the Barbarians.

concepts.title: Contemporary African Writing
concepts.contentHtml:
The 21st century has produced an extraordinary generation.

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (Nigerian, b. 1977): Half of a Yellow Sun, Americanah.

Maaza Mengiste (Ethiopian-American): The Shadow King.

NoViolet Bulawayo (Zimbabwean): We Need New Names, Glory.

Helon Habila, Teju Cole, Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor, Petina Gappah, Abdulrazak Gurnah (Tanzanian-British, Nobel 2021).

concepts.title: What 'Writing Back' Means
concepts.contentHtml:
The phrase 'writing back' describes the postcolonial gesture of responding to canonical European representations from the colonised perspective.

Examples: Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) tells the story of the 'madwoman in the attic' from Jane Eyre. Things Fall Apart writes back to Heart of Darkness implicitly.

The mode has been generative but is also limited. As postcolonial literatures have grown into self-sustaining traditions, the explicit 'writing back' move has become less central.

title: Indian Postcolonial
description: Rushdie, Roy, Ghosh — the great Indian English novel

concepts.title: R.K. Narayan and the Pre-Rushdie Generation
concepts.contentHtml:
Indian English fiction predates 1981. R.K. Narayan (1906-2001) wrote about the fictional South Indian town Malgudi across more than a dozen novels. His mode is quiet realist comedy with Hindu philosophical undertones.

Mulk Raj Anand, Raja Rao, Anita Desai, Nayantara Sahgal, Khushwant Singh formed the broader pre-Rushdie generation.

concepts.title: Rushdie's Midnight's Children
concepts.contentHtml:
Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981, Booker; later voted 'Booker of Bookers') changed the international perception of Indian English fiction.

Saleem Sinai is born at the moment of Indian independence (midnight, August 15, 1947). The 1,001 children born within India that hour have magical powers; Saleem's life and the nation's intertwine.

Style: maximalist, polyphonic, allusive, mixing English with Hindi/Urdu rhythms. Magical-realist in mode.

concepts.title: The Satanic Verses Affair
concepts.contentHtml:
Rushdie's The Satanic Verses (1988) provoked one of the major literary-political crises of the 20th century. Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa in February 1989 calling for Rushdie's death; Rushdie went into hiding for years; his Japanese translator was murdered, his Italian translator stabbed, his Norwegian publisher shot.

The fatwa was 'lifted' in 1998. In August 2022 Rushdie was stabbed at a public event and seriously injured; he survived.

concepts.title: Roy and the Booker Generation
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1990s saw the Indian English novel reach further global success.

Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things (1997) won the Booker.

Vikram Seth's A Suitable Boy (1993): 1,400 pages on post-Partition India.

Amitav Ghosh: The Shadow Lines, The Glass Palace, the Ibis Trilogy.

Rohinton Mistry: A Fine Balance (1995), Emergency-era India.

Kiran Desai's The Inheritance of Loss (2006, Booker).

concepts.title: Languages and Politics
concepts.contentHtml:
One persistent question: should serious Indian fiction be in English, or in regional languages?

The Indian English novel has dominated international perception. But the regional-language traditions are vast and largely untranslated.

Recent translation work has begun bringing more regional-language writing to wider audiences. Geetanjali Shree's Tomb of Sand (translated from Hindi by Daisy Rockwell) won the 2022 International Booker.

title: Caribbean & Diaspora
description: Walcott, Naipaul, Kincaid — island and exile

concepts.title: The Caribbean Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
The Caribbean is small in population but huge in literary output. The legacy of slavery, the multiple colonial powers, the diasporic patterns of subsequent emigration produce a literature unusually intense in its engagement with displacement and cultural mixing.

Major figures: Aimé Césaire, Édouard Glissant, Frantz Fanon (Martinique); C.L.R. James (Trinidad); George Lamming, Kamau Brathwaite, Derek Walcott; V.S. Naipaul, Sam Selvon (Trinidad); Jean Rhys, Jamaica Kincaid.

concepts.title: Walcott
concepts.contentHtml:
Derek Walcott (St Lucia, 1930-2017, Nobel 1992) was the great Caribbean poet. His verse fuses classical European reference with Caribbean idiom and landscape.

Major works: Another Life (1973); Sea Grapes (1976); Omeros (1990, his masterpiece — a 325-page epic poem mapping the Iliad onto St Lucian fishermen).

His combination of European technical formality with Caribbean material answered: could the colonised use the coloniser's tradition without subordinating themselves to it? His poems demonstrate yes — the tradition becomes new in their hands.

concepts.title: Naipaul
concepts.contentHtml:
V.S. Naipaul (Trinidad, 1932-2018, Nobel 2001) was the great Caribbean novelist of his generation — and the most controversial.

Major novels: A House for Mr Biswas (1961); The Mimic Men (1967); A Bend in the River (1979); The Enigma of Arrival (1987).

Naipaul's prose is widely admired. His political views were less so. Increasingly conservative, he made dismissive statements about postcolonial societies that struck many critics as colonial-condescension recycled.

concepts.title: Kincaid and Younger Voices
concepts.contentHtml:
Jamaica Kincaid (Antigua, b. 1949) brought a fierce, sustained anger about colonialism and family into her prose. A Small Place (1988) is a 100-page essay-novel addressed to the tourist destroying the very place they're enjoying.

Edwidge Danticat (Haitian-American, b. 1969).

Junot Díaz (Dominican-American, b. 1968): The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao (Pulitzer 2008).

Marlon James (Jamaican, b. 1970): A Brief History of Seven Killings (Booker 2015).

concepts.title: Theorising the Caribbean
concepts.contentHtml:
The Caribbean has produced major postcolonial theorists alongside its imaginative writers.

Édouard Glissant's Caribbean Discourse (1981) and Poetics of Relation (1990) developed concepts of creolisation and opacity (the right not to be fully comprehended by external categories).

Kamau Brathwaite theorised 'nation language' as the proper medium for Caribbean literature.

Stuart Hall (Jamaican-British) brought Caribbean perspective into British Cultural Studies.
